subtitle: Stop settling for software that almost fits. Build the one that does.
title: The Tolerance Tax
description: Stop settling for software that almost fits. Build the one that does.
body_html:
Every tool you use is a compromise someone else made for a million people, and you are one of them. You accept the 80% fit — the tab manager that’s ugly, the shortcut that’s mapped wrong, the setting that should exist and doesn’t — because building your own version was never worth it. That trade just broke, and most people haven’t noticed yet.

Here’s what noticing it looks like. I wanted a good tab extension. The one I actually liked had been dead since 2020, and everything still shipping annoyed me in some specific way — this one phoned home, that one looked like it was designed in 2013, none of them synced to anything I trusted. The old move is to pick the least-bad option and quietly resent it forever. Instead I built the exact one I wanted in about thirty minutes of my time. Not “learned to build it” over a heroic weekend. Thirty minutes of actually deciding things, while an agent did the typing. That gap is the whole story.

The tax you didn’t know you were paying

Call it the Tolerance Tax: the ongoing cost of living with software that almost fits. You pay it in tiny frictions, every single day, and you pay it precisely because the alternative — build the thing yourself — always cost more than the annoyance did. So the annoyance won. Not because you chose it, but by default, because the math never came out the other way.

That math is what changed. The price of “just build it” didn’t drop to zero, but it dropped below the threshold where tolerating the friction was the rational call. And once it crosses that line, the default flips. The honest answer to “I wish this worked differently” stops being a shrug and starts being: so change it. This afternoon.

Most people are still running on the old prices. They’ve internalized “building software is expensive” so deeply that they don’t even register the wants anymore — the friction just gets filed under how things are. That filing cabinet is the tax. And it’s full of stuff that’s now cheap enough to fix.

What I actually wanted, and what it took

I had four requirements, and nothing on the market hit all four. I wanted it fast and lightweight. I wanted it private — no accounts, no analytics, no server owned by a stranger. I wanted it to sync to something I controlled, so my data was mine. And I wanted it to look good, because I was going to stare at it every day.

So I built that. It’s about 120 KB. It syncs a snapshot of my lists to a private GitHub Gist on my own account — no third-party backend exists, because I didn’t build one and didn’t want one. No login. No tracking. It reads on my phone through a little companion page. It does exactly the four things I wanted and nothing I didn’t, because there was no product manager, no roadmap, and no other user to design around. There was me.

The cost of all that was roughly thirty minutes of my attention: deciding what it should do, looking at what came back, and saying “no, the header goes here” a few times. I made every product call. The agent handled the part that used to be the project — the actual construction.

Look at the difference. The dead extension I was replacing, next to the one I made for myself:

Left: the extension I was replacing. Right: the one I built for myself.

The one on the right is prettier, and I want to be clear that’s not vanity. “Looks the way I want” used to be the first thing you sacrificed — the negotiable that got cut the moment building got hard. Now it’s free. When the thing only has to please you, and making it please you costs half an hour, you stop settling on aesthetics too.

Why this is a different default, not a faster one

The temptation is to read this as “building got faster.” It did, but that undersells it. Speed alone doesn’t change behavior — a 20% discount on something you weren’t going to buy is still a no. What changed is that an entire category of wants became actionable at all.

Think about your own “would be nice but not worth it” list — the workflow you’ve hand-patched for years, the feature a vendor keeps refusing to ship, the tool that’s so close but wrong in one maddening way. That list wasn’t defined by what you wanted. It was defined by what building cost. Every item on it is there because the payoff didn’t clear the old price. Reprice the building, and the list mostly empties.

And here’s the part that’s genuinely new: the thing you build doesn’t have to justify itself to a market. It doesn’t need a million users, or a hundred, or one besides you. It only has to be worth your thirty minutes. Software built for exactly one person used to be an absurd indulgence — all that effort for an audience of one. Now it’s just the natural size of a want. Bespoke is the cheap option.

Where the tax didn’t actually go to zero

I’m not going to pretend the thirty minutes was magic, because it wasn’t, and the interesting part is why. It worked because I knew exactly what I wanted and could tell immediately when it came back wrong. The building got cheap. The deciding didn’t.

You still need enough judgment to steer — to know that the header’s in the wrong place, that this feature is bloat, that the sync model should push to a Gist and not a server. That’s real, and it’s not nothing. But steering is a much lower bar than building, and it’s a bar most people who use software all day can already clear. If you’ve ever had a strong opinion about a tool being wrong, you have the input this requires. (That opinion, it turns out, is now the scarce part — but that’s its own conversation.)

What to do with this

Go open your “would be nice but not worth it” list — you have one, even if it’s not written down. Every item on it was priced under the old rules. Pick one and notice that it’s now a weekend, or an afternoon, or thirty minutes. Then actually build it, because the list was never the point; clearing an item off it is.

Stop grading your personal tools on whether they’d survive as products. They don’t need to. A tool that fits one person perfectly and would fail in a market is not a failed product — it’s a successful tool. The market test was always about someone else’s economics, and you’re not in that business.

And the next time something you use is wrong in a way you’ve learned to ignore — the friction you route around on autopilot — catch yourself doing it. That workaround is a receipt. You’ve been paying the Tolerance Tax on that exact thing, maybe for years, and the reason you’re still paying is that you haven’t updated the price.

title: I spent 30 minutes a week finding NYC events. Now I don’t.
description: For a while, I had this mildly annoying recurring task: scan a bunch of event newsletters, check a couple of websites, mentally track the things that sounded interesting, and then inevitably lose half of them before the week was out.
body_html:
For a while, I had this mildly annoying recurring task: scan a bunch of event newsletters, check a couple of websites, mentally track the things that sounded interesting, and then inevitably lose half of them before the week was out. Maybe 30 minutes a week, spread across context switches. Not a crisis. Just friction.

I automated it. The whole thing took about two hours to build. Now a markdown file shows up in my Obsidian inbox every Tuesday morning with that week’s events, pre-classified by whether I’d actually want to go. I check a few boxes, move the file, and my activities list updates itself. I spend more time at events now. I spend zero time looking for them.

Here’s what I built and what I learned doing it.

How it works

Three sources feed the system: email newsletters (one of them sends 50+ events per email), a handful of websites I used to check manually — The Skint, TimeOut NYC, Secret NYC — and a webhook I can trigger from Telegram or an iOS Shortcut when I stumble on something worth tracking.

Each source is a thin n8n workflow that does one thing: fetch content, strip HTML, pass a standardized payload downstream. All the actual intelligence lives in a central Event Processor workflow that passes data to a local Ollama instance running llama3.1:8b on my Mac Mini. It extracts structured event data from the raw text, classifies each event as work or social, high or low interest based on a preference config, and runs three-layer deduplication so I never see the same event twice. The whole thing costs $0 to run. Local LLM, no API calls.

The output is a markdown file in my Obsidian inbox. Checkboxes for each event. I review it on my phone, check what looks interesting, move the file to a Processed folder. An n8n workflow watches that folder, reads my selections, appends them to my Activities page, and marks everything else as skipped.

The most interesting design decision in the whole system is that last part — using the filesystem as a review queue. Instead of building a custom UI for human-in-the-loop review, I write a file, annotate it, and move it. n8n watches the folder. Obsidian syncs across all my devices via LiveSync. The “interface” is just a file on my phone. I’m planning to reuse this pattern for email summaries and CRM follow-ups — anything that needs a judgment call before automation acts.

How I built it

About two hours total, split roughly half between writing specs and half building. The honest version: I wish I’d spent more time on the spec, because I had to build the thing twice.

The first pass had architectural gaps I only caught mid-build. The second pass, with tighter specs, went to a different tool and produced a working deployment without the same rework. The specs were the same. The agent was different. The specs survived; the agent didn’t matter.

That’s the part I keep thinking about. When you’re building with AI assistance, the spec is the durable artifact. The model, the tool, the session — those are ephemeral. A well-written spec is something you can hand to a different tool, a different model, or a future version of yourself, and still get to a working result. A vague spec just means you’re debugging someone else’s interpretation of what you wanted.

What this actually requires

I want to be honest about the ceiling here. What I built isn’t a weekend ChatGPT project. It runs on n8n (self-hosted), a local LLM, and Obsidian with LiveSync. There’s a real gap between “comfortable using AI chatbots” and “building automations with AI help,” and I’m not going to pretend that gap is zero.

But it’s smaller than it looks. The actual building — once I had good specs — was mostly directing an AI agent through implementation, not writing code by hand. The leverage comes from knowing what you want clearly enough to describe it, and being comfortable enough with these tools to debug when something breaks.

The 30 minutes I was spending manually scanning event sites every week was a spec waiting to be written. Most recurring tasks are.

Three things worth taking from this

  • Recurring friction is a spec in disguise. If you’re doing something manually on a schedule, you already know the inputs, the outputs, and what good looks like. That’s most of the spec.

  • Spend longer on the spec than feels necessary. I built this twice because I didn’t. The time you save rushing into implementation you pay back in rework.

  • The agent is ephemeral; the spec survives. Write it like you’re handing it to someone else — because eventually you will be.

subtitle: A Mental Model for Working With AI
title: The 5 Levels of AI-Powered Productivity
description: A Mental Model for Working With AI
body_html:
I’ve been experimenting with building a personal AI toolstack — basically trying to figure out how to use AI as a core part of how I get things done. Along the way, a lot of friends have started asking me about it. “How do I actually use this stuff?” “What should I be doing with AI?” Same conversation, over and over.

So here’s my attempt at organizing my thinking. (And yes, I used AI to help me write this — the ideas are mine, the drafting was a team effort. That’s kind of the whole point.)

This is a mental model for how AI fits into personal productivity — not as a single tool you adopt, but as a spectrum of how deeply it integrates into the way you work.

Level 0: Passive AI

You’re already here, whether you know it or not. Autocorrect, spam filters, Gmail’s suggested replies, Spotify recommendations — AI is embedded in the tools you use every day. You accept or reject its suggestions without thinking about it. This is the baseline — AI works on you, not for you.

Level 1: Ad Hoc Prompting

This is where most people who say they “use AI” actually sit. You open ChatGPT or Claude, ask a question, maybe paste in some text to summarize or rewrite. It’s conversational and one-off — you get your answer and close the tab. There’s no system, no repeatability.

The benefit: You can move faster on individual tasks — drafting, brainstorming, research, debugging. Things that used to take an hour take minutes.

The toolstack: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini — whichever chatbot you prefer. Maybe Perplexity for research.

Level 2: Deliberate Workflows

Instead of ad hoc prompting, you build repeatable AI workflows. You create custom GPTs for recurring tasks. You save prompt templates. You learn which models are better at which types of work and route accordingly. You might use structured output formats or chain multiple prompts together.

The shift: AI becomes a tool in your system, not a novelty you reach for occasionally. You’re designing how you interact with it, not just reacting.

The benefit: Consistency and speed compound. Tasks that you do regularly — weekly reports, email drafts, content creation — get dramatically faster because you’ve already solved how to prompt for them.

The toolstack: Custom GPTs, saved prompt libraries, Claude Projects, workflow templates. You start caring about model selection.

Level 3: Agentic Actions

This is the level where the AI stops just advising and starts doing. Through APIs, integrations, and automation platforms, the AI can take actions on your behalf — sending emails, updating databases, creating documents, triggering multi-step automations. You delegate tasks, not just questions.

The shift: You move from “what should I do?” to “go do this.” The AI executes, not just responds. This is where trust becomes the bottleneck — you have to be comfortable letting the AI act, not just suggest.

The benefit: Entire categories of work start happening without you. Repetitive operational tasks — data entry, follow-ups, file organization — can run on autopilot.

The toolstack: Automation platforms like n8n or Zapier with AI integrations, API connections to your SaaS tools, AI coding assistants that can execute tasks.

Level 4: AI-Native Stack

At this level, the AI isn’t just connected to your tools — it lives in them. It has persistent context about your projects, your contacts, your files, your priorities. You’re not handing off context at the start of every interaction; the agent already knows what you’re working on. You work side by side, like a colleague who’s always up to speed.

The shift: From per-task delegation to continuous collaboration. The AI doesn’t just do what you ask — it can surface things you haven’t thought to ask about, because it has the context to reason about your work holistically.

The benefit: You stop being the bottleneck for your own information. The AI can connect dots across your projects, remind you of commitments, and proactively suggest next steps.

The toolstack: Interconnected local tools with shared data layers — think knowledge bases, CRMs, and project management tools that your AI agent can read and write to continuously. OpenClaw or Claud Code with extra setup. It’s possible to still use online SaaS products, but that also becomes a bottleneck for your AI-Agents (i.e. probably worth switching from Notion to Obsidian, but Gmail can stay).

Level 5: Self-Extending System

The AI doesn’t just use your tools — it builds new ones. You describe a need or a friction point, and the agent creates the automation, the integration, or the workflow to solve it. Your productivity system evolves without you having to architect every piece of it.

The shift: The AI moves from executor to builder. Instead of operating within the system you’ve designed, it helps design the system itself. You find yourself asking for diagrams about how ‘your’ current infrastructure is set up.

The benefit: Your setup improves faster than you could improve it alone. Friction points get solved as they appear, not whenever you find time to sit down and engineer a fix.

The toolstack: OpenClaw, AI coding agents with access to your infrastructure, plus the ability to deploy and test their own creations. This is the bleeding edge.

So where does this leave you?

Most people today are somewhere between Level 0 and Level 1. The real leverage starts at Level 2, and the hardest jump is from 2 to 3 — because it requires both trusting AI to act on your behalf and some technical setup (API keys, automation platforms, integration configs) that most people don’t want to deal with yet.

If you don’t want to do the legwork, just wait a bit. Every level is getting productized. Companies are already packaging Level 2 workflows into apps. Level 3 automations are getting no-code interfaces. The gap between what’s possible and what’s accessible shrinks every month. If you can’t/won’t set up this stuff yourself, you’ll be able to buy it off the shelf soon enough.

I’m actively building and experimenting at Levels 4 and 5. In future posts, I’ll go deeper into what that actually looks like in practice — the tools, the architecture, and the tradeoffs.

My first post here covered the toolstack setup that I’m using to facilitate this stuff.

If this framework is useful to you, follow along.

subtitle: A practical guide to rebuilding your productivity system for the agent era
title: How I Rebuilt My Personal Tool Stack to Be Fully AI-Literate
description: A practical guide to rebuilding your productivity system for the agent era
body_html:
AI agents are getting scarily capable. They can write code, research topics, analyze documents, and reason through complex problems. But ask one to do something simple with your actual workflow — check your calendar, file a note, create a task in the right project — and it hits a wall.

The problem isn’t the AI. It’s your tools.

Most productivity software was built for humans clicking through GUIs. That’s fine for you, but it makes your entire system invisible to an agent. If you want AI to go from “chatbot I consult” to “co-worker who operates alongside me,” you need a tool stack that’s built for both of you.

This guide explains how.

What Makes a Tool “AI-Literate”

The core concept is legibility — can an agent read, understand, and act on the data inside your tools? This is the single lens you should use to evaluate every tool in your stack.

Four principles determine legibility:

  • Structured data beats blobs. A markdown file with clear headers is infinitely more useful to an agent than a rich-text document with embedded widgets. The agent can parse, search, and modify markdown. Rich text is a black box.

  • APIs beat GUIs. If the only way to interact with a tool is through a browser, an agent either can’t use it or has to use it clumsily through screen automation. A clean API means the agent operates the tool as fluently as you do.

  • Open formats beat proprietary ones. If your data lives in a format only one app can read, you’ve created a bottleneck. SQLite, markdown, JSON, CSV — these are universally legible.

  • Local-first beats cloud-only. When data lives on a machine you control, an agent running locally can access it directly — no auth flows, rate limits, or API costs.

Most popular productivity tools fail at least two of these. That’s why a purpose-built stack matters.

The Design Principles

Before picking tools, commit to four rules:

  1. Agent-interactable. Every tool must expose an API or a local data format an agent can operate. No GUI-only tools allowed.

  2. Agent-improveable. The agent shouldn’t just execute your workflows — it should be able to modify, extend, and optimize them. This means your automation layer itself must be agent-accessible.

  3. Modular. Any single tool can be swapped without breaking the rest of the system.

  4. LLM-agnostic. Don’t lock into one AI provider. Models change fast. Your infrastructure should outlast any single one.

The Stack: Layer by Layer

Here’s a reference stack that follows these principles. Your specific tools may differ — what matters is that each layer meets the legibility bar.

Task Management → Todoist (Doist). Well-documented REST API, natural language input, simple data model. An agent can create tasks, query what’s due, and reorganize priorities programmatically.

Calendar → Google Calendar. Not the most exciting choice, but the API is battle-tested and every agent framework supports it. This is one area where a major cloud tool wins — the ecosystem support outweighs the benefits of self-hosting.

Databases → NocoDB + SQLite. NocoDB is an open-source Airtable alternative that runs on top of a standard database. Use it for structured data: CRM contacts, project trackers, reference tables. Underneath it’s SQLite, so an agent can also query data directly with SQL. Two interfaces to the same data — GUI for you, API or raw SQL for the agent.

Notes & Knowledge → Obsidian + LiveSync + CouchDB. This is the most important choice in the stack. Obsidian stores everything as plain markdown files in a local folder. No database, no proprietary format — just .md files an agent can read, search, create, and modify with basic file operations. LiveSync backed by CouchDB handles cross-device sync without any data leaving your network.

Agent Layer → OpenClaw (or your framework of choice). This is the orchestrator that connects to everything above. OpenClaw supports multi-model routing, a plugin-based memory system, and runs persistently. But the specific framework matters less than the principle: you need a central agent layer that can reach every other tool.

Automation → n8n. Self-hosted workflow automation — think Zapier, but you own it. n8n is the glue: meeting transcripts get processed into action items, new contacts trigger follow-up sequences, recurring reports compile themselves. Critically, n8n’s workflows are stored as JSON and it exposes its own API — meaning an agent can not only trigger workflows but create and modify them. This is what makes the whole system agent-improveable.

Remote Access → Tailscale. Secure mesh networking between devices. Access every service from anywhere without exposing anything to the public internet.

Backup → Syncthing. Decentralized file sync. No cloud intermediary. If your server dies, everything important is already replicated.

Meeting Transcription → Meetily → n8n. Meetily handles transcription. The output pipes into n8n, which parses it, extracts action items, creates tasks, and files the transcript in Obsidian. One meeting generates five downstream effects without you touching anything.

What You Can Do With This

The stack above might sound over-engineered until you see what it enables. These are the kinds of interactions that become possible when every tool is legible to an agent:

Cross-system memory. “What have I been working on with Sarah, and what articles have I read that relate to that?” The agent queries your CRM, searches your notes, pulls relevant clippings, and synthesizes a briefing. One question, four data sources, zero tab-switching.

Synthesized daily briefings. “What should I focus on today?” The agent checks your calendar, pulls overdue tasks, scans recent notes for open threads, and generates a prioritized rundown.

Research synthesis. “Summarize everything I’ve saved about [topic] and draft a rough take.” The agent searches across your notes and clippings, identifies key themes, and produces a synthesis. An hour of re-reading compressed into seconds.

Self-improving workflows. “I keep manually copying action items from meeting transcripts. Fix that.” The agent examines your pipeline, identifies the gap, and builds a new n8n workflow to handle it automatically. The system literally improves itself.

Pre-meeting prep. “Prepare me for my call in 30 minutes.” The agent pulls the calendar event, finds the contact record, surfaces prior notes, and compiles a brief. Five minutes before the call, you know everything you need to know.

None of these require a single new AI capability. They just require tools that an agent can actually read and write to.

Takeaways

Optimize for legibility, not features. The best tool isn’t the one with the slickest UI — it’s the one your agent can operate most fluently. That’s a fundamentally different way to evaluate software.

Shift your mental model. Stop asking “what tools do I want to use?” and start asking “what tools can my agent use?” Every tool choice becomes a question of interoperability.

The tools will change. The principles won’t. Specific products come and go. But legibility, modularity, agent-interactability, and agent-improveability will only matter more as agents get more capable. Build for the interface, not the implementation.

But ask one to do something simple with your actual workflow — check your calendar, file a note, create a task in the right project — and it hits a wall.
